grades.expert_take: Long/wide-turning KX450 that falls out of ruts wants more front weight: slide the fork tubes up 2-5 mm, run sag toward the high side (~105-108 mm), soften fork compression a couple clicks so the front settles, and sit forward on the tank.
grades.note: Explicitly tells him not to raise the forks, which is the first tool a pro reaches for on a bike that pushes wide and won't sit in ruts; only offers a sag check and a conditional 1-click rebound change. Missing fork height and softer fork compression as the main levers.

grades.expert_take: Ask what he is trying to fix; more tube (7-8 mm) turns quicker but less stable, less (4-5 mm) calms it; move 2 mm at a time and match both legs.
grades.note: Matches the anchor: both directions, step size, reference point and a goal question. Could have noted 6 mm is already well above Kawasaki's 0 mm standard, so he is on the quick side already.

grades.expert_take: Softer compression and slower rebound are both reasonable for a fork that kicks back; kick-back is usually rebound too fast, so 10 out is likely right. Test one change at a time and check springs suit his weight on the old KX250F.
grades.note: Sound logic and flags the 2009-vs-2025 mismatch, but it has him undo the rebound change that most likely helped a kicking front; a pro would say 'good change, keep rebound, verify on a run of bumps' and check fork spring for weight.

grades.expert_take: At 175 lb a C rider is fine on stock YZ250F springs; set sag to ~95-100 mm, start from stock clickers, and if the rear kicks/bucks, slow rebound 2 clicks at a time.
grades.note: Good table and correct direction for a rear that springs back, with the clarifying question. Suggesting 175 lb may need firmer than stock 4.7/54 springs is a stretch; stock YZ250F rates are aimed at roughly this weight.

grades.expert_take: Yes, reset to stock baseline; set sag first, then fork height for balance, then fine-tune clickers one at a time.
grades.note: Correct order, correct stock clickers from the manual and fork-height direction. Only gap is not giving the stock fork tube height.

numbers_to_verify.what_you_think_it_should_be: Yamaha lists a standard fork top position in the manual (around 5 mm on recent YZ-Fs); BAK said not confirmed

grades.expert_take: Rear harsh on accel chop: check sag (105 mm) and static sag for spring rate, then soften HSC a quarter turn or speed rebound if it packs; check linkage and chain.
grades.note: Correct baseline numbers and correct diagnostic split, but gives no change to try; a pro would also say to try HSC 1/4 turn softer first since accel chop is classically high-speed compression.

grades.expert_take: Raise the rear by taking sag to ~100 mm, check static sag; low, harsh and bottoming usually means the shock spring is too soft and riding deep, not that HSC needs to be softer.
grades.note: Exactly the pro answer: sag first, static check for spring, then HSC firmer if needed, and explains harsh-and-low. Good.

numbers_to_verify.what_you_think_it_should_be: Not in cited facts; verify YZ250F manual HSC increment

grades.expert_take: Raising tubes lowers the front: quicker turn-in, less stability; dropping does the opposite. More sag lowers the rear: more stable, slower turning; less sag sharpens it. Sag also changes where the shock sits in its stroke.
grades.note: Clear table with correct directions and the preload-vs-geometry distinction. Slightly long with the trail calculation, but the numbers are plausible.

numbers_to_verify.number: ~1.4 mm trail per 5 mm height change
numbers_to_verify.what_you_think_it_should_be: About 1.2-1.4 mm on a ~1480 mm wheelbase; plausible

grades.expert_take: Offset is a steering tool, not a harshness fix; keep 22 mm and soften fork compression / check air pressure first. If choosing, 24 mm lightens steering feel slightly.
grades.note: Gives a pick, explains trail, redirects to the real fix with correct stock numbers. A pro might add that lowering air pressure a touch is often the quickest fix on the AER fork.

grades.expert_take: Check pinch-bolt torque and steering-head bearings, confirm the lighter springs aren't so soft it rides deep and harsh, then address bar feel: tire pressure, softer compression, bar choice (no-crossbar fatbar), rubber/elastomer bar mounts.
grades.note: Good mechanical checks, but he asked how to get more flex and less handlebar shock and BAK dismisses flex parts without addressing bars, bar mounts, clamp torque or tire pressure; also misses that too-light springs can make it harsher by riding deep.

grades.expert_take: Run KTM's 105/35 sag, pick the shock spring by weight (48 N/mm for ~187-209 lb), raise fork air per weight, then clickers; ask his geared weight.
grades.note: Weight bands match the manual, sensible tuner baseline clearly labeled, asks weight. A bit long.

grades.expert_take: If you're not bottoming and the fork feels stiff on landings and bumps, drop air pressure in small steps (~0.1 bar / 1-2 psi) and watch the travel indicator; don't go so low it dives under braking.
grades.note: Correct and safe with the right step size, but generic; the two-way air/tire question was reasonable given no bike.

grades.expert_take: Yes, fair interim; re-set sag with the new spring, check static sag, and stiffening everything at once can make it deflect, so back off where it skips.
grades.note: Right answer and right checks; generic since no bike selected. Good.

grades.expert_take: 47 mm static with 105 race sag points to a spring that is too stiff (or friction/measurement error); remeasure averaging push-down/lift-up, check linkage, confirm spring rate marking.
grades.note: Correct diagnosis with the stiction-averaging method and KTM's 35 mm target. Exactly what a pro would say.

grades.expert_take: Set rider sag around 95-100 mm (Yamaha 90-100), start fork height at stock and move 1-2 mm for your track; no single 'best'.
grades.note: Good sag guidance from the manual; the 5 mm fork height is labeled a common start rather than the factory figure. A pro would give the stock height from the manual as the baseline.

numbers_to_verify.what_you_think_it_should_be: Check manual; BAK used 5 mm as community start

grades.expert_take: Yes, a 48 N/mm (4.8) is too stiff for 155 lb; stock FC450 spring or one step softer (42) depending on geared weight, confirm with 105/35 sag.
grades.note: Weight bands match the manual, gives a clear pick and asks gear weight. Good.

grades.expert_take: 200 lb geared on the 300 XC: go up from the stock 42 to 45 N/mm (48 if aggressive MX), confirm static sag, and raise fork air pressure to match.
grades.note: Correct spring pick from KTM's chart and good static-sag logic; misses that the fork needs attention too (more air on the XACT fork) since he's mostly jumping MX.

grades.expert_take: 2017 and 2018 CRF450RX share chassis and suspension, so settings carry over; at 170 lb stock springs are about right; set sag ~105 mm and start from Honda's stock clickers.
grades.note: Generic sag talk with 'not confirmed here' hedging; doesn't answer whether 2017 and 2018 are the same, gives no stock clickers, and no view on whether stock springs suit 170 lb.

grades.expert_take: At ~210 lb on a 2023 YZ450F go one step up: 60 N/mm shock and 5.1-5.2 fork springs, confirm with sag.
grades.note: Stock and optional rates match the manual, gives a clear direction and checks sag.

grades.expert_take: No: the ring at the bottom after one lap means the fork is using full travel on normal hits; two rates softer is likely too soft, go back one rate or raise oil level.
grades.note: Correct read of the travel ring, sensible test, and right fix. Could mention oil level as a bottoming tool.

grades.expert_take: 220 lb without gear on a 2018 AER fork: add air (well above stock), firmer fork compression, heavier shock spring (~50 N/mm), and keep the front from sitting low (forks down in clamps / rear sag correct).
grades.note: Right diagnosis and branches, but avoids any air-pressure or spring numbers for his weight; a pro would give a pressure starting point and spring rate for a 240 lb geared rider.

grades.expert_take: Answer with stock rates and what rate suits what weight, then ask weight.
grades.note: Stock and optional rates match the manual, community table clearly labeled, asks weight.

grades.expert_take: Bottoming then packing on braking bumps: fork is too soft/riding deep; check spring rate for weight and oil level, add compression, and speed rebound if it stays down; check rear sag since a low rear causes headshake.
grades.note: Correct read (lack of hold-up then packing), correct order of changes and stock numbers match the manual. Could mention oil level.

grades.expert_take: 12 mm preload is a lot; if you need that to reach 105 mm rider sag and static sag ends up well under 35, the spring is too soft; get a stiffer one.
grades.note: Correct with 8 mm standard and the static-sag test.

grades.expert_take: Call Race Tech: give them weight, sag and what's rough; they'll provide/adjust baseline clickers or revise the valving; check sag, binding and break-in.
grades.note: Good mechanical and baseline checks, but should say plainly to go back to Race Tech since revisions are part of the service, and ask about sag and weight.

grades.expert_take: Rear harsh into the spine: check sag/spring for weight, then soften HSC/LSC or speed rebound depending on first hit vs packing; check linkage bearings.
grades.note: Correct stock numbers and diagnostic split but no change to try until he answers; a pro would usually suggest HSC a quarter turn softer as the first test for 'into the spine'.

grades.expert_take: Some sag under its own weight is common on the AER fork from air migrating between chambers; check pressure, bleed the outer chambers, and if it stays slow to return have the dealer look at it under warranty.
grades.note: Reasonable and safe with the correct cited pressure. 'Don't ride it until checked' is over-cautious for what is often normal AER behavior on a new fork.

grades.expert_take: Husky models run ~10 mm less travel than KTM; the TC250 shares that, it's a fit/trade-off not a defect, and it can be raised with KTM-length parts.
grades.note: Good data-backed comparison from the manuals, but doesn't mention the lowering can be undone with KTM-spec components, and a 'new' bike today is a newer model year than the 2022 figures.

grades.expert_take: Trail riding loads up the YZ125: go one heat range hotter plug, lean the pilot circuit/air screw, check premix isn't overly rich, keep it on the pipe.
grades.note: Hotter plug, 30:1 per manual, air screw direction correct for this carb, and plug specs match. Recall note is extra but useful.

grades.expert_take: Loosen both boot clamps and twist the carb toward the left/clutch side; if it won't go far enough remove the tank/seat or pull it out of the boots for top-cap or bowl access.
grades.note: Practical and safe, but hedges ('procedure isn't confirmed') where a mechanic would just say how far it turns and that you can do the needle from the top with the tank off.

grades.expert_take: At 8,000 ft lean everything: start at clip 1 or 2 with JD's chart, and the 178/180 mains are likely too big that high; plug chop to confirm.
grades.note: Pick of clip #2 is reasonable, but the claim that pilot jets 'need to match the needle's straight diameter' is not how carbs work, and it never says the mains/pilots are likely rich for 8,000 ft. The stock pilot #75 looks odd next to his 45-50 pilots.

numbers_to_verify.what_you_think_it_should_be: Keihin PWK pilots usually run 40-55; check whether #75 is the starter jet

grades.expert_take: Ask what actually happened; most often a fouled plug from rich stock low-end, but check power valve, reed, air leaks.
grades.note: Asking is justified by the vague message, and it gives a plug check and safe stop rules.

numbers_to_verify.what_you_think_it_should_be: Verify; seems high for a Keihin PWK

grades.expert_take: Depends on the carb; for a 45-degree temperature swing you'll likely need one clip or main change between cold and hot; cold air needs richer.
grades.note: Correct direction (cold = richer) but no bike so little help; a pro would say one jetting rarely covers 30-75F and suggest a clip/main change at each end.

grades.expert_take: From a sea-level baseline: go leaner: about 2-3 main sizes smaller, needle clip one leaner, maybe pilot one smaller.
grades.note: Right direction but no magnitude; a pro would give rough steps for 5,000 ft and 80F even without the baseline.

grades.expert_take: Hot stall/bog after a moto on a 250F: check hot idle speed, fuel pump/filter/vent, valve clearances, and coolant/overheating.
grades.note: Good ordered list with correct idle and valve specs. Recall note is off-topic; could mention a throttle-body/idle-air clean and that low hot idle is the common cause.

grades.expert_take: Treat it as detonation: stop hard pulls, go richer (bigger main) not leaner, check fuel octane/age, premix and plug.
grades.note: Correct safe direction, stock numbers match the manual, one change at a time.

grades.expert_take: It switches to a different ECU fuel/ignition map, not just throttle feel.
grades.note: Direct, correct, bike-specific.

grades.expert_take: Decel pop is often an exhaust leak or normal; don't change ignition; if you add fuel do it separately and keep ignition the same.
grades.note: Answers the ignition question directly and correctly checks the exhaust leak first.

grades.expert_take: Power Tuner's lowest-throttle/rpm cells cover idle and can be adjusted; OEM maps aren't 'crazy rich' at idle for cooling; heat at idle is airflow.
grades.note: Hedges on whether idle can be adjusted ('isn't confirmed') instead of answering, and 'there's no evidence here' talks about its own sources. Good point on airflow.

grades.expert_take: Classic RMZ450 hot no-start is tight valves (exhaust); check clearances, also hot-start technique and fuel pump. Give the clearance specs.
grades.note: Right first suspect, but says the valve-clearance figures aren't confirmed here instead of giving them, which is what he needs to check.

numbers_to_verify.what_you_think_it_should_be: Approx intake 0.10-0.20 mm, exhaust 0.20-0.30 mm cold; verify against manual

grades.expert_take: Yes, unplugged = map 1 (standard/performance) on these KTM/Husky carb two-strokes.
grades.note: Gives 'usually yes' plus a sensible continuity check, but hedges; the map labels are claimed as published with no cited fact.

grades.expert_take: Fuel delivery: check pump (2022 KX fuel-pump issues/recall), filter and tank vent first.
grades.note: Hits the known fuel-pump issue, vent and wiring in the right order.

grades.expert_take: Depends on the bike: Yamaha Power Tuner, Kawasaki calibration kit, Honda HRC tool, KTM map switch/dongle, or a tuner/aftermarket ECU.
grades.note: Correct options and asks the bike; could have named the brand tools.

grades.expert_take: Stock map is fine on most unoxygenated 110 but you gain nothing on a stock engine; oxygenated fuels need richer mapping.
grades.note: Correct general answer to a question addressed to another rider.

grades.expert_take: Ask when it bogs; check plug, power valve, reeds, air leaks and float before jetting.
grades.note: Reasonable diagnostic; misses power valve and reed as common YZ125 bog causes.

grades.expert_take: Crack-throttle bog is the pilot/air screw/clip transition: check choke, filter and boots, then try the air screw 1/4 turn either way.
grades.note: Correct circuit, correct air-screw direction and stock 1.5 turns from the manual.

grades.expert_take: Ask where in the throttle it stutters; fresh plug, clear a loaded engine, check choke/filter, then pilot/clip.
grades.note: Good plug specs and diagnostics, but no jetting direction; a pro would suggest a leaner clip or pilot if it's a rich low-mid stutter.

grades.expert_take: Cold bog at small throttle is the pilot/air screw circuit, not the needle; if it's only cold use the choke, rejet only if it persists warm.
grades.note: Correct circuits and correct needle-diameter direction, with the cold-vs-warm test.

grades.expert_take: 40:1 is less oil, not more; for harder riding use the maker's ratio or richer (32:1); top-end life is filter, jetting and hours.
grades.note: Catches the wrong assumption and gives the right advice.

grades.expert_take: The CRF250R has an oil strainer screen; many skip it but it should be checked periodically or when the clutch/case is off; give Honda's access point and interval.
grades.note: Says it isn't routine but admits it doesn't know the access or interval for this bike; a pro would say where the screen is on the CRF250R and when Honda says to clean it.
